subtitle: Develop an equity committee with a clear purpose, approved work time and defined authority. Practice sharing responsibilities, coordinating existing efforts and reporting what changes for people served.
audience: For DHS and DSD leaders, executive sponsors, committee chairs, unit equity team members and facilitators who set up, run or support equity committees.

lessons.title: Purpose, charter and decision rights
objectives: Distinguish an advisory equity committee from a decision-making body and from formal offices such as EOAD and Human Resources.
Draft the core elements of a committee or unit equity team charter.
Identify where a committee's work connects to state and agency equity commitments.
Plan a decision-rights map that states what the group decides, recommends, is consulted on and is informed about.
lessons.teaching:
An equity committee needs agreement about its work and the decisions its members can make. Without that agreement, useful proposals may remain unanswered while members take on work outside their authority. A charter gives the group and its sponsor a common reference for setting goals, arranging time and resolving questions.

Connect the charter to the agency's duties. Executive Order 23-12 continued the One Minnesota Council and the Governor's Community Council and described support for agency equity plans. It assigned an annual report to the One Minnesota Council, not every local committee. Check the order's current status when applying it. The published DHS Equity Policy gives equity directors and area equity committees roles in putting the policy into practice. It includes committee actions and legislative proposals among the uses of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit.

A useful charter states the group's purpose, scope, member selection, terms, sponsor, reporting plan and review date. Describe the work time needed and obtain approval from the people who control that time and budget. The charter records approved plans; it does not by itself authorize pay, overtime, position changes or decisions reserved to another office. For each activity, say whether the group decides, recommends, gives advice or receives information. A team might set an approved meeting agenda while proposing a notice change for the program manager's decision.

Name the formal routes for complaints, accommodations, grievances, legal questions and Tribal consultation. Being a committee member does not give someone authority to investigate conduct or decide these matters. Follow the applicable Human Resources, Equal Opportunity and Access Division, labor relations, ADA, legal or Tribal liaison process. Sharing a contact is useful, but members must also meet their own reporting duties. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations to Human Resources or the affirmative action officer. DHS policy also requires prompt referral to Equal Opportunity and Access. Address urgent protection needs through the responsible office without waiting for a committee meeting or charter review.
lessons.keyPoint: Record the committee’s approved authority, resources and referral paths. A charter does not replace formal reporting duties or grant powers reserved to another office.
lessons.example: Practice case: The newly formed equity team in a DSD policy unit has met four times. At the latest meeting, Lwazi reports that a colleague asked the team to look into how a supervisor treated her in a performance conversation. Rebecca, a team member, suggests the group interview the people involved. The team has no charter yet, and the executive sponsor, Carlos, has only attended the first meeting. Lwazi has already made the required report through the agency process; the committee is deciding how to respond without taking over that process.
lessons.question: What should the team do next?
choices: Interview the people involved, since the team was formed to address equity problems and staff are trusting it.
Explain to the colleague that concerns about individual treatment go to EOAD or Human Resources, share how to reach them, and draft a charter with Carlos that makes referral paths explicit.
Ask Carlos to decide whether the supervisor acted fairly and report back to the team.
feedback: The team has no authority or process to investigate, and doing so could harm the colleague, the supervisor and any formal process. Good intentions do not create investigative authority.

This is the strongest response after the required report has been made. Share the formal contact route, avoid a committee investigation and clarify the charter with Carlos. Any member with further reporting or protection duties must fulfill them promptly.
An executive sponsor is not a substitute for the formal complaint process, and routing the concern this way still bypasses the offices responsible.
lessons.reflection: If you serve on or lead an equity group, could every member state in one sentence what the group decides and what it only recommends? Privately note where you would guess differently from your colleagues.
lessons.action: Draft a one-page charter or charter revision using the job aid headings. Fill in the decision-rights section for at least four kinds of work, list the formal offices the group refers to, and ask your executive sponsor to review it.

check.question: Which item belongs in an equity committee charter's list of things the group does not do?
check.correct: Investigate complaints about an individual employee's conduct.
wrong: Recommend changes to a notice template.
Review data on how a process performs for different groups.
check.feedback: Committee membership does not confer investigative authority. Follow the agency’s designated investigation process; authorized process review and recommendations can remain within a committee’s charter.

lessons.title: Membership without extracting unpaid labor
objectives: Explain the minority tax and how it can appear in equity committee work.
Identify membership practices that spread workload and protect members' core responsibilities.
Distinguish an equity committee from an employee resource group and a labor-management committee.
Draft a workload agreement between a member and a supervisor.
lessons.teaching:
Committee work takes time that otherwise would go to another task. When leaders invite participation without adjusting assignments, members may face conflicting expectations about their regular work and their committee work. Discuss those demands before selecting members, and revisit them when service needs or committee commitments change.

In a 2015 discussion article, Rodriguez, Campbell and Pololi examine the minority tax in academic medicine. They describe unequal diversity duties and work that may receive little credit when faculty seek promotion. The authors discuss a term already in use; they do not claim to have created it. This offers a question for state workplaces: who is repeatedly asked to contribute, and how is that work supported? It does not establish a local pattern by itself or tell you what an individual colleague experiences. Examine assignments and ask about capacity without inferring a person's needs from identity.

Arrange approved work time through a written agreement that names hours, coverage and duties that will change. Seek Human Resources or labor relations guidance where pay, position duties or a labor agreement is involved. Do not rely on a charter alone to authorize those changes. If adequate capacity is unavailable, reduce the scope or obtain a resourced schedule before assigning more work. Recruit beyond the usual volunteers, invite colleagues with relevant authority and use rotating terms where continuity allows. Give the work credit through approved development and recognition plans. This program’s learning activities do not replace formal employee reviews.

No member represents every person who shares an identity or experience. Invite interest, skills and relevant work perspectives without pressuring colleagues to disclose personal histories. That practice does not cancel a separate lawful duty to provide information. When community input is needed, offer accessible ways for people affected to contribute. A staff member’s views cannot replace formal consultation between governments, arranged through the Tribal liaison.

Keep the group's purpose distinct from other structures. MMB's enterprise employee resource groups are employee-led networks with their own rules, including sponsors, bylaws and work plans. Their guidelines bar bargaining over employment terms or handling grievances. They also state that these groups do not replace labor-management committees. An equity committee's authority comes from its approved agency role; it should coordinate with these groups without assuming their functions or treating their members as an unlimited source of labor.
lessons.keyPoint: Agree on approved time, coverage and a manageable scope before assigning committee work. Share responsibility without treating identity as expertise or expecting one person to represent a community.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ayaan manages a DSD unit and is forming a unit equity team. Three staff volunteer, all of whom already serve on other equity efforts and two of whom recently told Ayaan their caseloads feel heavy. A senior analyst, Beth, has not volunteered. Ayaan wonders whether to accept the three volunteers as the team and move quickly, because the division director has asked every unit to have a team in place by next month and nobody else has come forward on their own. Ayaan can obtain approval to reassign duties and provide paid committee time; any launch still depends on confirming that coverage.
lessons.question: What is the best next step for Ayaan?
choices: Accept the three volunteers, since they have the most experience and enthusiasm.
Postpone the team until workloads are lighter across the unit.
Set up the team with paid time and a written workload agreement for each member, invite a wider group including Beth, and use rotating terms.
feedback: Speed would come at the cost of concentrating more unrecognized work on people who are already stretched. That repeats the pattern the team is meant to address.

An indefinite delay leaves the resource problem unresolved. Here, approved workload changes are available, so Ayaan should pursue them. If safe coverage cannot be arranged, reducing the scope or changing the schedule is appropriate.

This is the best response when paid time and coverage are approved before the work begins. Invite wider participation, agree on the duties that will move and use terms that share responsibility while maintaining continuity.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider whether committee contributions are visible in workload discussions. What approved adjustment would recognize the time involved and protect essential responsibilities?
lessons.action: Draft a workload agreement with one member and their supervisor. Include expected hours, coverage, duties to adjust, term length and recognition. Obtain any required Human Resources or labor approvals before implementing changes.

check.question: According to MMB's enterprise ERG guidelines, which statement is accurate?
check.correct: Employee resource groups cannot replace labor-management committees.
wrong: ERGs are the official body for agency equity analysis of legislation.
ERGs replace the need for agency equity committees.
check.feedback: MMB guidelines describe ERGs as employee-led groups with bylaws, work plans and executive sponsors, and state that they cannot replace labor-management committees. Agency equity committees, ERGs and labor-management committees have different purposes and authority.

lessons.title: Activity inventory and action plans
objectives: Draft an inventory of equity-related activities already underway in a division or unit.
Compare activities against agency priorities to find gaps and duplication.
Plan an action with a clear change, owner, resources and review date.
Explain why a short list of owned actions is stronger than a long list of ideas.
lessons.teaching:
Before proposing new work, identify relevant activity already underway in the division or unit. A DSD policy team might be reviewing guidance while a communications team tests notice wording and a data team examines response patterns. Record each activity's owner, focus, intended change, current status and available evidence. Use information the committee is authorized to access, and keep individual case or personnel details out of a general coordination inventory.

An inventory can suggest overlapping work, unmet needs and efforts whose ownership is uncertain. It does not prove duplication: two teams may serve different populations or have separate requirements. Confirm what you find with the responsible owners before recommending a change. Compare the work with agency priorities and the state Equity Analysis Toolkit's questions about intended results, engagement, evidence and accountability. Describe missing information so readers can distinguish a verified gap from an unanswered question.

Choose commitments that match the group's authority and available resources. A long list may be useful as a record of suggestions, but it is not a promise to implement everything. For each proposed action, name the specific change, accountable owner, partners, required time and resources, first milestone, measure and review date. Obtain the responsible leader's agreement before assigning their team work. If resources are uncertain, record that dependency and the decision needed rather than presenting the action as funded. Keep other suggestions visible and explain how priorities were selected.

Plan accessible engagement while participants can still influence the design. A service notice change might require perspectives from people receiving services, county partners, interpreters and disability advocates. Explain how feedback will be considered and report back in a form participants can use. Coordinate data collection and sharing with the responsible privacy and records staff rather than assuming consent permits every use.

Where a proposal may have Tribal implications, involve the DHS Tribal liaison early and follow the agency's consultation process. Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 requires timely, meaningful consultation with the affected Tribal governments and consideration of that input in agency decisions. General outreach, an advisory meeting or a staff member's contribution does not fulfill that formal relationship. The committee can identify the need and support coordination while authorized officials carry out consultation.
lessons.keyPoint: Map what already exists before adding work, then commit to a few owned, resourced actions with a review date, and plan engagement with the people affected from the start.
lessons.example: Practice case: Fatima chairs a division equity committee that has collected forty-two ideas from a staff survey. Members are excited and want to adopt them all. Fatima also knows that a data team is already building disaggregated reports and that a communications unit is revising notice templates. Leslie, the executive sponsor, has said she can support two or three priority actions with staff time this year.
lessons.question: What should Fatima propose?
choices: Build an inventory of current activities, connect with the data and communications teams, and select two or three actions with owners, resources and review dates that Leslie will support.
Adopt all forty-two ideas as the committee's work plan so no staff member feels unheard.
Ask the data and communications teams to stop their work so the committee can coordinate everything centrally.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It avoids duplication, matches commitments to the resources the sponsor can actually provide and keeps the other ideas visible for later.
A forty-two item plan without resources sets the committee up to fail and can erode staff trust more than a short, honest list.
The committee has no stated authority to stop those teams’ work. Confirm overlap with the owners and coordinate recommendations through the responsible leaders before proposing a change.
lessons.reflection: Think about equity-related efforts you know of in your area. Privately, which ones have a clear owner today, and which may have quietly lost one?
lessons.action: Start an inventory using authorized information and the job aid fields. Identify several current activities, then confirm one possible overlap, unmet need or ownership question with the responsible people before raising a recommendation.

check.question: What is the main purpose of an equity activity inventory?
check.correct: To map existing work so the group can find duplication, gaps and orphaned efforts before adding new actions.
wrong: To rate which employees are contributing most to equity work.
To replace the agency equity plan with a committee plan.
check.feedback: An inventory is a map, not a performance tool. It supports coordination with the agency plan and helps a committee choose a small number of well-placed actions.

lessons.title: Accountability measures and executive sponsors
objectives: Distinguish measures of processes and outcomes from measures that score or rank individuals.
Draft two accountability measures for a committee action.
Identify the responsibilities of an executive sponsor and how a committee escalates a stalled decision.
Plan a regular report that is honest about what changed and what did not.
lessons.teaching:
A committee needs evidence about the commitments it made and the effect of its work. Attendance can show participation, but it cannot establish that service access improved. For this program, use measures of processes and results rather than creating personal equity scores or competitive participation rankings. This learning approach does not replace required training records, authorized workforce evaluation or other official reporting responsibilities.

Process measures describe whether an agreed action occurred, such as testing revised notices with readers before release. Outcome measures describe results, such as the share of notices receiving a response by the deadline. Those results may improve, remain unchanged or worsen, and a change alone does not establish its cause. Experience measures add what people affected report about using the process. Consider these sources together instead of treating one favorable number as proof of success.

For each measure, record its source, baseline, population, time period, review frequency and responsible interpreter. Explain the denominator behind a rate, missing information and other changes that could affect comparison. Disaggregate results only through authorized data practices, and protect small groups from identification. When seeking feedback, explain its purpose, use and privacy limits, with participation choices appropriate to that process. Consent alone does not authorize otherwise restricted collection, access or disclosure.

The sponsor connects recommendations to the people authorized to decide and resource them. Agree on how the sponsor receives proposals, responds to unresolved decisions and explains a declined recommendation. A sponsor may also hold a supervisory role, but those responsibilities should remain clear rather than being assumed from the sponsor title. The role does not replace Human Resources, Equal Opportunity and Access, legal counsel or other designated offices.

When a decision stalls, provide a brief written account of the requested change, evidence, options, proposed owner and date needed. Explain the practical effect of delay and ask the sponsor to route matters beyond the committee's authority. Urgent reporting or protection duties continue through their formal channels. Set a reporting schedule in the charter; an annual account can be useful, but it is a program recommendation unless an applicable policy requires it. Report what happened, what remains uncertain and what decision comes next, using information approved for the intended audience.
lessons.keyPoint: Use measures to examine actions and results, including uncertainty and adverse changes. Ask the sponsor for decisions within the proper authority and report progress without overstating the evidence.
lessons.example: Practice case: An equity committee wants to show progress to division leadership. Jamal proposes a public chart ranking each unit by how many staff attended equity trainings. Wren suggests instead tracking two things for the notice-redesign action: whether revised notices were tested with readers before release, and whether the rate of on-time responses changes across language groups. The sponsor, Mei, has asked for a report next month.
lessons.question: What should the committee bring to Mei?
choices: Both proposals, letting Mei choose which one to publish.
Wren's process and outcome measures, with the baseline, data limits and a recommendation on what decision is needed next.
Jamal's ranking chart, because attendance is easy to count and will motivate units to compete.
feedback: Explain why attendance rankings do not answer whether the notice redesign improved access. Recommend measures connected to the action rather than leaving that distinction unexplained for Mei to resolve.

This is the best response. It connects measures to the notice action and identifies the next decision. Explain data limits and report any improvement, deterioration or uncertainty without assuming the redesign caused the result.
Attendance counts can support authorized participation reporting, but a competitive ranking does not establish better notice access. Use measures that address the stated service change.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a measure at work that changed behavior in a way nobody intended. What did it reward, and what would a better measure have looked at instead?
lessons.action: For one committee action, write one process measure and one outcome measure. For each, name the data source, baseline, review frequency and one limit. Draft a one-paragraph recommendation to your sponsor naming the decision you need and by when.

check.question: Which is an example of an outcome measure for an equity action on notices?
check.correct: Change in the on-time response rate to a notice across language groups.
wrong: The number of staff in each unit who attended an equity workshop.
A ranking of units by the number of equity activities they reported.
check.feedback: A change in response rates describes an outcome, whether favorable or adverse. Interpret it with the baseline, denominator and data limits; attendance alone does not establish that the notice process improved.

cards.back: An approved agreement about purpose, scope, membership, work time, sponsor, decision rights, reporting and formal referral paths.
A statement, for each kind of work, of whether the group decides, recommends, is consulted or is informed.
A concept discussed in academic medicine concerning unequal, often unrecognized responsibilities assigned to underrepresented faculty. Examine local workload evidence before applying the analogy.
A coordination record of existing work, ownership, intended results, status and evidence. Confirm possible overlap or gaps with owners before drawing conclusions.
A leader who carries the group's recommendations to decision-makers, secures time and resources, removes barriers and explains decisions back to the group.

aid.heading: Charter checklist
items: Purpose in one or two sentences and the scope it covers.
Membership, selection, fixed terms and rotation.
Approved work time, coverage and supervisory agreement, with any required Human Resources or labor review.
Decision rights for each kind of work: decide, recommend, consulted, informed.
Formal referral paths and immediate reporting duties; committee membership alone does not authorize investigations or formal consultation.
Executive sponsor, reporting line and charter review date.

aid.heading: Fair membership
items: Agree on time and coverage before assigning work; reduce scope or adjust the schedule if capacity is unavailable.
Recruit beyond the usual volunteers, including people with positional power.
Do not pressure members to disclose identity or speak for a whole community.
Use accessible community engagement and the separate formal Tribal consultation process where applicable.

aid.heading: Inventory and action plan fields
items: Activity, owner, population or process affected, intended change, status, evidence.
For each action: specific change, owner, partners, resources, first milestone, measure, review date.
Engagement plan for people affected, including Tribal liaison involvement where relevant.

aid.heading: Accountability without scoring people
items: Connect process, outcome and experience measures to the action; preserve required official reporting.
State source, baseline, denominator, population, frequency, interpreter and limits; use authorized data practices.
Bring written recommendations with a decision date to the sponsor; continue urgent formal reporting duties.
Agree on a reporting schedule and explain results, uncertainty and next decisions using information approved for the audience.

sources.title: Office of the Governor — Executive Order 23-12, Providing Equitable, Inclusive, and Effective Government for All (Legislative Reference Library copy)
sources.note: Supports the renewal of the One Minnesota Council and the Governor's Community Council, references to agency-specific equity plans and the long-range plan, and annual reporting. Executive orders can be amended or rescinded; check current status.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Equity Policy
sources.note: The published policy assigns equity directors and administration or area equity committees implementation responsibilities and includes committee actions among uses of the DHS toolkit. Confirm applicable internal procedures before implementation.

sources.title: Rodriguez, Campbell and Pololi — Addressing disparities in academic medicine: what of the minority tax? BMC Medical Education (2015)
sources.note: A 2015 discussion article about responsibility disparities in academic medicine. The course uses it as an analogy for examining workload, not evidence of a particular state workplace or individual experience.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Enterprise Employee Resource Groups (ERGs) Guidelines
sources.note: Supports the description of ERGs (executive sponsors, bylaws, work plans) and the statement that ERGs cannot replace labor-management committees.

sources.title: Office of Equity, Opportunity, and Accessibility — Equity Analysis Toolkit
sources.note: The state toolkit supports examination of intended outcomes, engagement, evidence and accountability. Its planning questions do not confer staffing, funding or data authority.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 — Government-to-government relationship with Tribal governments
sources.note: Supports the statement that DHS is among agencies required to have a Tribal consultation policy and a Tribal liaison and to consult on matters with Tribal implications.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations to Human Resources or the agency affirmative action officer.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation
sources.note: Describes employee reporting, supervisory protection and prompt referral responsibilities, and designated Equal Opportunity and Access functions.
